title: Periodic Motion and Oscillations

standard_text: Periodic motion: period and frequency; simple harmonic motion of springs and pendulums; displacement, velocity and acceleration in SHM; energy in oscillations; damping and resonance. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, Physics 1, Quarter 2)

key_sub: T = 2π√(m/k) for a mass on a spring.
body_html:
How to think about it

Periodic motion repeats at regular intervals. The period T is the time for one cycle; frequency f = 1/T. In simple harmonic motion the restoring force is proportional to displacement and points back toward equilibrium, as in a mass on a spring or a pendulum with small swings.

For a pendulum T = 2π√(L/g), so the period depends on length, not mass. For a spring T = 2π√(m/k). In SHM, energy changes between kinetic and potential; damping removes energy, and resonance happens when a system is pushed at its natural frequency.

Example

A pendulum makes 20 swings in 40 s. Period?

40 ÷ 20

Answer: 2 s

Example

The pendulum's length is made 4 times longer. New period?

T ∝ √L

Answer: twice as long

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a heavier pendulum bob swings slower.
  • Mixing up period and frequency.
  • Thinking speed is greatest at the ends of a swing.

faq.q: Why do bridges and buildings need damping?
faq.a: To prevent large oscillations from wind or earthquakes at resonance.

faq.q: Where is a pendulum moving fastest?
faq.a: At the lowest point, where kinetic energy is greatest.
